caption: "new cat species" — 200,000+ searches this week. Swipe for 10 things most people don't know about the first new cat in a century.

Why: on September 17 a study in Current Biology named Leopardus tilcayo, a spotted cat smaller than a house cat, from Bolivia's Yungas cloud forest. Researchers call it the first new living wild cat species in over 100 years.
What most people don't know: a man handed one to a sanctuary thinking it was a kitten. He had fed it noodles, rice and eggs. Its line split from the other tiger cats about 1.4 million years ago.
Very simply put: cat species number 42 was living on noodles, and nobody knows how many are left.

slides.headline: The first new wild cat in *a century*, found in Bolivia.
slides.sub: 10 things most people don't know about Leopardus tilcayo, 200,000+ searches this week.

slides.headline: It is called *tilcayo*, the local name for generations.
slides.sub: Formally Leopardus tilcayo, named in Current Biology on September 17. The word has no meaning in Quechua or Aymara.
slides.image: Dense green cloud forest canopy with mist rolling between trees on a steep Andean slope, canopy in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain soft mist, photorealistic, no people, no text

slides.headline: Smaller than a house cat: about *1.4 kg*.
slides.sub: About 46 cm long, light brown with dark rosettes and rounded ears.
slides.image: A small spotted cat curled asleep on a wooden bench in soft daylight, cat in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain wooden bench, photorealistic, no text

slides.headline: It lives in the *Yungas*, where the Andes meet the Amazon.
slides.sub: Bolivian cloud forest near La Paz. Camera traps show it hunts at night; its scat shows small rodents.
slides.image: Steep forested Andean valley with clouds pouring over a ridge at sunrise, ridge in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain cloud, photorealistic, no people, no text

slides.headline: A man brought one to a sanctuary thinking it was a *kitten*.
slides.sub: He had fed it noodles, rice and eggs. Two now live at the Senda Verde refuge.
slides.image: A bowl of plain cooked noodles and rice on a rustic wooden table in warm light, bowl in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain wood, photorealistic, no text

slides.headline: DNA from *two* animals proved it is a species.
slides.sub: The study compared 38 cats, including 8 museum specimens, from across South America.
slides.image: Rows of small labelled glass vials in a laboratory rack under cool white light, vials in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain white bench, photorealistic, no readable text

slides.headline: Its line split from other tiger cats *1.4 million years* ago.
slides.sub: Tiger cats are now five species across South America. The same paper named a new subspecies in Peru.
slides.image: A spotted ocelot-like cat walking along a fallen log in dappled forest light, cat in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain leaf litter, photorealistic, no text

slides.headline: No museum had a specimen. Nobody knows *how many* are left.
slides.sub: Its cloud forest is shrinking as farming and development move in, the authors warn.
slides.image: A cleared hillside with tree stumps next to standing cloud forest under a grey sky, hillside in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain bare earth, photorealistic, no people, no text

slides.headline: Science counted *41* cat species before this one.
slides.sub: From the rusty-spotted cat, under 1 kg, to the tiger. Formal IUCN recognition is pending.
slides.image: A row of small carved wooden cat figures in different sizes on a white shelf, figures in the upper half of the frame, lower half plain white, photorealistic, no text
